title: The signals that matter
summary: Lag and its growth, age of the oldest message, ready versus unacked, redeliveries, dead letters, under-replicated and offline partitions, disk and memory alarms: what each one tells you and where to read it.

steps.title: Where the signals live
body: Most messaging dashboards have fifty graphs and the incident is in none of them. A short list answers the three
questions on-call asks: **are we keeping up, are we losing or looping on messages, is the broker healthy?**
```text
publish rate                 queue depth: ready | unacked  deliver / ack rate
publish errors / nacks       consumer lag (records) and its GROWTH RATE
confirm latency              age of the oldest message (lag in TIME)
redelivery rate, DLQ depth
under-replicated / offline partitions, ISR shrinks
disk free, memory alarm, flow control (RabbitMQ)
- **Lag in records** says how much is waiting; its **growth rate** says whether you are falling behind (positive)
or recovering (negative). A lag of 50 000 that shrinks by 500/s is fine; a lag of 2 000 that grows all night is not.
- **Lag in time** (age of the oldest unprocessed message, or lag / consume rate) is what users feel: "invoices are
12 minutes late". Alert on that, not on a record count that means different things per topic.
- **Ready vs unacked** (RabbitMQ): *ready* waits for a consumer; *unacked* is delivered but not yet acknowledged.
High unacked with ready near 0 means consumers hold messages they are not finishing.
- **Redeliveries** and **DLQ depth**: a poison message loop shows up as a high redelivery rate long before the DLQ.
> **See it:** in **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka**, play *Lag keeps growing*.

steps.prompt: Match each signal to what it tells you.
pairs: Consumer lag growth rate > 0 for 15 minutes
Consumers process slower than producers write
How late the work is, in the unit users feel
Consumers hold messages they do not finish
Messages are nacked or consumers crash, often a poison loop
Followers are not keeping up with leaders
Publishers on every connection are being blocked
explain: Each of these points to a different first action: scale or fix consumers, find the poison message, or look at broker
health. That is what makes them good signals.

steps.title: Lag trend and time to drain
prompt: Write two methods behind every lag panel.
- `double GrowthPerSecond(List<(long TimeMs, long Lag)> samples)`: the change in lag per second between the **first**
and the **last** sample (negative when recovering); 0 with fewer than two samples.
- `double? SecondsToDrain(long lag, double producePerSec, double consumePerSec)`: how long until the lag reaches 0 at
these rates: 0 when there is no lag, `null` when consumers are not faster than producers (it never drains),
otherwise `lag / (consumePerSec - producePerSec)`.
starter: double GrowthPerSecond(List<(long TimeMs, long Lag)> samples)
double? SecondsToDrain(long lag, double producePerSec, double consumePerSec)
solution: double GrowthPerSecond(List<(long TimeMs, long Lag)> samples)
double? SecondsToDrain(long lag, double producePerSec, double consumePerSec)
hints: Use `samples[0]` and `samples[^1]`; divide the lag difference by the time difference in seconds (`/ 1000.0`).
`SecondsToDrain`: check `lag <= 0` first, then whether consumers are faster at all.
template: Dojo.Eq("growing 50 records per second", 50.0, GrowthPerSecond(new List<(long TimeMs, long Lag)> { (0, 1000), (60000, 4000), (120000, 7000) }));
Dojo.Eq("recovering", -100.0, GrowthPerSecond(new List<(long TimeMs, long Lag)> { (0, 9000), (30000, 6000) }));
Dojo.Eq("one sample has no trend", 0.0, GrowthPerSecond(new List<(long TimeMs, long Lag)> { (0, 5) }));
Dojo.Eq("no lag, nothing to drain", (double?)0, SecondsToDrain(0, 500, 100));
Dojo.Eq("consumers no faster than producers: never", (double?)null, SecondsToDrain(1000, 500, 500));

steps.title: RabbitMQ: depth, alarms and flow control
body: What to watch on a RabbitMQ 4.x node, and where it comes from:
| Signal | Prometheus (`rabbitmq_prometheus`, port **15692**) | CLI |
| ready / unacked per queue | `rabbitmq_queue_messages_ready`, `rabbitmq_queue_messages_unacked` | `rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages_ready messages_unacknowledged consumers` |
| publish / deliver / ack / redeliver rates | `rabbitmq_global_messages_received_total`, `..._delivered_total`, `..._acknowledged_total`, `..._redelivered_total` (use `rate()`) | management UI |
| dead-lettered | `rabbitmq_global_messages_dead_lettered_*_total` | DLQ depth via `list_queues` |
| memory / disk alarms | `rabbitmq_alarms_memory_used_watermark`, `rabbitmq_alarms_free_disk_space_watermark` | `rabbitmq-diagnostics check_local_alarms` |
- `/metrics` returns metrics **aggregated** per node (cheap); per-queue metrics are on `/metrics/per-object` or
`/metrics/detailed?family=queue_coarse_metrics`. Scraping per-object on a node with 50 000 queues is expensive.
- **Memory alarm** at `vm_memory_high_watermark.relative` (0.6 of RAM by default) and **disk alarm** below
`disk_free_limit` (default 50 MB, far too low for production) **block every publishing connection** in the cluster
(`connection.blocked`), while consumers keep running. Producers see publishes hang, not errors.
- **Flow control**: before the alarm, RabbitMQ slows fast publishers per connection (state `flow` in the UI).
Many connections in `flow` means the node cannot keep up with ingress.
- Long queues are the root of most RabbitMQ pain: keep them short (consumers keep up), or bound them with
`x-max-length` + `x-overflow` and alert on depth growth.

steps.prompt: The billing team says "RabbitMQ is slow". Which queue shows the actual problem, and what is it?
code: $ rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages_ready messages_unacknowledged consumers
options: `billing`: 2 000 delivered but unacknowledged to one consumer, nothing ready: the consumer is stuck (or has a huge prefetch) and holds the messages
`audit`: 3 ready means the consumer is too slow
RabbitMQ itself is overloaded, because the total is over 2 000
explain: `billing` has one consumer holding 2 000 messages it has not acknowledged, and nothing waiting. Either the handler hangs
(a blocked database call, a deadlock) or prefetch is very high and the consumer is slow. Next: `rabbitmqctl
list_consumers queue_name prefetch_count ack_required`, then the consumer's thread dump and logs. Restarting the
consumer returns all 2 000 to *ready* with `Redelivered = true`, so the handler must be idempotent.

steps.prompt: A lag of 90 000 records, consumed at 1 500 records per second. What does the dashboard's "time lag" panel show?
explain: 90 000 / 1 500 = 60 seconds. Converting lag to time makes alerts comparable across topics: 90 000 records is a minute
here and a week on a topic that gets 10 records an hour.

steps.title: Kafka: replication health and broker resources
body: Broker metrics come over **JMX**; scrape them with the Prometheus JMX exporter java agent on every broker.
Consumer lag comes from a separate exporter (for example `kafka_exporter`: `kafka_consumergroup_lag`) or from the
consumer clients themselves.
| JMX metric | Healthy | When it is not |
| `kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=UnderReplicatedPartitions` | 0 | a follower is down or slow: disk, network, GC, a dead broker |
| `kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=UnderMinIsrPartitionCount` | 0 | `acks=all` writes to those partitions are **failing now** |
| `kafka.controller:type=KafkaController,name=OfflinePartitionsCount` | 0 | partitions without a leader: nothing can read or write them |
| `kafka.controller:type=KafkaController,name=ActiveControllerCount` | exactly 1 across the controllers | 0 = no metadata changes possible |
| `kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=IsrShrinksPerSec` / `IsrExpandsPerSec` | near 0 | flapping replicas: an overloaded broker or network |
| `kafka.server:type=KafkaRequestHandlerPool,name=RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent` | > 0.3 | the broker is saturated |
| log dir disk usage (`kafka-log-dirs.sh --describe`, node exporter) | < 70-80% | a full disk takes the log dir offline |
The CLI equivalents for a quick look:
```bash
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --under-replicated-partitions
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --under-min-isr-partitions
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --unavailable-partitions
kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 describe --status

items: Queue with 0 ready, 20 unacked, 1 consumer with prefetch 20
Lag of 300 records, flat all day, on a busy topic
Redelivered rate is 30% of the deliver rate
Several publishing connections stuck in state `flow`
explain: A small, **stable** lag and a full prefetch window are normal steady state. Trends and flapping are what matter:

steps.title: Triage the CLI output
prompt: On-call pastes the output of two commands. Turn it into findings.
Write `List<string> Triage(string[] listQueues, string[] topicDescribe)`.
**`rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages_ready messages_unacknowledged consumers`**: data lines have 4 tab-separated
fields with numbers in the last three; skip every other line (the `Timeout:` and `Listing` lines and the header). For
each queue, in order, the first rule that applies:
1. name ends with `.dlq` and holds messages (ready + unacked > 0) → `"orders.dlq: 37 dead letters"`
2. ready > 0 and no consumers → `"email: 18000 ready and no consumers"`
3. unacked >= 1000 → `"billing: 2000 unacknowledged (consumer stuck or prefetch too high)"`
4. ready >= 10000 → `"search-index: backlog of 25000 ready"`
**`kafka-topics.sh --describe`**: partition lines contain the tokens `Partition:`, `Leader:`, `Replicas:` and `Isr:`,
each followed by its value (split on spaces and tabs); other lines are skipped. For each partition, in order:
1. `Leader:` is `none` or `-1` → `"orders-2: OFFLINE (no leader)"`
2. fewer ISR members than replicas → `"orders-1: under-replicated, isr 2 of replicas 2,3,1"`
Queue findings come first, then partition findings. No findings at all → `["all clear"]`.
solution: if (f.Length != 4 || !long.TryParse(f[1], out var ready) || !long.TryParse(f[2], out var unacked) || !int.TryParse(f[3], out var consumers))
if (name.EndsWith(".dlq") && ready + unacked > 0) findings.Add($"{name}: {ready + unacked} dead letters");
else if (ready > 0 && consumers == 0) findings.Add($"{name}: {ready} ready and no consumers");
else if (unacked >= 1000) findings.Add($"{name}: {unacked} unacknowledged (consumer stuck or prefetch too high)");
else if (ready >= 10000) findings.Add($"{name}: backlog of {ready} ready");
return i >= 0 && i + 1 < t.Count ? t[i + 1] : null;
if (leader is "none" or "-1") { findings.Add($"{name}: OFFLINE (no leader)"); continue; }
if (isrCount < replicaCount) findings.Add($"{name}: under-replicated, isr {isr} of replicas {replicas}");
return findings.Count > 0 ? findings : new List<string> { "all clear" };
hints: Queues: `line.Split('\t')`, then `long.TryParse` the three numbers; lines that do not parse are skipped.
Topics: split on spaces and tabs, then find the token `"Leader:"` and read the next token. An empty `Isr:` is followed by the next key (`Elr:`).
Use `if / else if` so each queue gets at most one finding.
template: "billing: 2000 unacknowledged (consumer stuck or prefetch too high)",

Dojo.Eq("a healthy system", new List<string> { "all clear" }, Triage(new[] { "name\tmessages_ready\tmessages_unacknowledged\tconsumers", "orders\t0\t12\t4", "orders.dlq\t0\t0\t0" }, new[] { dojoTopics[0], dojoTopics[1] }));
Dojo.Eq("empty input", new List<string> { "all clear" }, Triage(new string[0], new string[0]));
